title: Shraddha Kapoor Posted a Dance Video at 40. The Internet Told Her She Was Too Old. Here's Why That Matters.
excerpt: The Stree 2 star shared a goofy clip dancing to Michael Jackson. The backlash revealed everything that's still wrong with how Indian culture treats women who age.
body:
The video was innocent enough.

Shraddha Kapoor, 40, posted a short clip of herself dancing — freely, goofily, without choreography — to a Michael Jackson track on her social media. She wasn't promoting a film. She wasn't launching a product. She was just dancing because she felt like it.

The internet's response was depressingly predictable. Comments poured in calling her "too old" to be dancing like that, questioning whether a woman her age should be behaving so "casually," and offering the kind of unsolicited life advice that Indian women receive from the moment they turn 30: settle down, act your age, be dignified.

As Hauterrfly put it in their headline: "Internet Seriously Needs A Hobby."

The Double Standard That Never Dies

Shraddha Kapoor is not a newcomer trying to establish credibility. She is one of Bollywood's most commercially successful actresses. Stree 2, her 2024 horror-comedy, earned over ₹627 crore at the Indian box office, making it the second-highest-grossing Bollywood film of that year. She has been a leading lady in Hindi cinema for over a decade.

None of that mattered when the trolls decided she was too old to dance on her own Instagram.

The double standard is glaring. Akshay Kumar is 58 and continues to perform action sequences. Shah Rukh Khan is 60 and romances actresses half his age on screen. Salman Khan, 60, takes off his shirt in every other film and nobody blinks. But a 40-year-old woman dances to Michael Jackson and she's supposed to feel embarrassed?

This isn't a new phenomenon, but its persistence is the point. In Bollywood, male stars are allowed to age into "legend" status. Their grey hair becomes distinguished. Their slower pace becomes gravitas. Female stars, meanwhile, are pushed into "mother" roles the moment they cross 35 — if they're offered roles at all.

Why the Diaspora Should Pay Attention

For Indian women in the diaspora, Shraddha's trolling hits close to home. The ageism that governs Bollywood's treatment of its actresses is a mirror of the same pressure that Indian women face in their own communities — in Silicon Valley living rooms, in Diwali party conversations, in WhatsApp family groups.

The message is the same everywhere: after a certain age, Indian women are supposed to become invisible. They should stop being fun. They should stop being seen. They should, above all, stop being themselves.

It's the reason so many NRI women in their 30s and 40s talk about feeling caught between two cultures — the Western one that tells them to embrace aging, and the Indian one that tells them to disappear into it. Shraddha Kapoor dancing on Instagram shouldn't be controversial in 2026. The fact that it is says everything about how far Indian society still has to go.

The Bigger Picture

Shraddha's moment comes at a time when Bollywood is slowly — very slowly — beginning to reckon with its ageism problem. Madhuri Dixit, 59, is headlining Netflix's upcoming Maa Behen alongside Triptii Dimri. Tabu, 55, remains one of the industry's most sought-after actresses. Vidya Balan, 47, continues to carry films on her shoulders without relying on a male co-star.

These women are the exceptions, not the rule. But they represent a shift that the industry needs to embrace more fully — and that audiences need to support more vocally.

The trolls who came for Shraddha Kapoor over a 15-second dance video will have moved on by tomorrow. They always do. But the attitude they represent — that Indian women have an expiration date on their right to be joyful — is one that deserves to be challenged every single time it surfaces.

Shraddha Kapoor is 40. She's dancing. And she doesn't owe anyone an apology for either of those facts.
nri_angle: The ageism Shraddha faced mirrors pressures NRI women experience in their own communities — expectations to 'act your age,' disappear from public life after 35, and conform to cultural norms around aging that clash with Western values of self-expression. Bollywood's treatment of its actresses is a cultural export the diaspora consumes and internalizes.
author: Diaspora Desk
